items.summary: Persuasion is ordinary in a negotiation; the dark part is using it to hide the real price, the real stock or the real deadline. After reading this you can name nine techniques, say what the honest version of the same request is, and prepare the two things that protect you: your alternative and your walk-away price.
items.title: Dark Psychology in Business and Negotiation

items.summary: Professional email is a written register with its own rules: a subject line that gets opened, a structure the reader can scan, and a tone that survives being read without your voice. After reading this you can write a clear request, a careful apology, a firm refusal and a follow-up, and you will know the words each of them needs.
items.title: Writing Professional Emails in English

items.summary: Every workplace has a layer of language that is not in the dictionary: phrases for a meeting, a delay, a mistake, a decision. After reading this you will understand the expressions you hear in offices, use them at the right moment, and avoid the ones that make you sound either too casual or too managerial.
items.title: Understanding Common Workplace Expressions

items.summary: An interview introduction is not a biography. It is a short, structured answer that tells the interviewer who you are, why you are relevant and what you want next. After reading this you can prepare a 60-second introduction, describe your experience with evidence, ask questions that show judgement, and close the interview and follow up in a way that is remembered.
items.title: How to Introduce Yourself in a Job Interview

items.summary: A request for a raise is a business case, not a favour. It works when you arrive with evidence, a number and a calm plan. After reading this you will know when to ask, how to build the evidence, how to say the sentence out loud, and what to do in the week after you hear no.
items.title: How to Ask for a Raise Politely
